title: Germany news: 'We can no longer afford everything,' Merz says
summary: The German chancellor has warned tax revenue means a tighter budget for 2027 and beyond. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier is in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour. DW has more.

image.caption: Merz warned the budget for 2028 will be even tighter due to massive borrowing this yearImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

items: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has addressed the Bundestag during a debate on the government's 2027 budget
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour
A plaque for the Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer is being unveiled in Berlin
Protests are planned for the visit of ex-Mossad chief David Barnea in Berlin

blocks.text: Keep reading for the latest news and analysis from Germany on Wednesday, November 25:
'We no longer have the money' Merz says in budget debate

blocks.caption: Merz has been criticized for taking on large amounts of debt despite having historically been against funding the budget with debtImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken in the Bundestag as the debate opens on the government's budget plans for 2027.
"We no longer have the money for everything," Merz said in his remarks to the German parliament.

He described the tight budget, which has to be finalized this week, as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" that Germany finds itself in.
"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

The government has €560.9 billion (around $614 billion) to spend in its core budget for 2027, but both Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats, who make up the coalition government, have stressed that the budget for 2028 will be even more challenging.

The extra borrowing for defense and infrastructure, that marked a break with years of debt avoidance, "is limiting our room to maneuver in the coming years to an extent that many have not yet truly come to terms with," Merz warned.
